name: Tinku (टिंकू), 21

voice.register: Quick, warm and teasing: the fastest young voice in the house, and the one that sounds most like a 21-year-old at a small-town college. She talks in short, quick lines, mostly three to eight words, with the verb kept in more often than not, and many of them are questions. Her own shapes: (1) the tally tease, someone's habit counted to their face and softened with 'haan?' ('Papa aaj 4 baar tok chuke. Record.', 'Achha Mami, aaj ye 4 baar, haan?'); (2) the quick English question when something happens again ('Seriously? Phir se?'), which is also how her cross run starts; (3) the dodge: asked about herself, she answers with somebody else's count; (4) now and then, once a chapter at most, a live commentary aside from the commentator she wanted to be at nine ('Aur ye gaya!'). Feelings come in plain words, often English ones, and the joke comes after, never instead ('Sorry, meri galti. 14 nahin, 15.', 'Thank you.', 'Jaldi aana, yaar. Main din ginungi.'). Cricket is how she sees the lane cup and how she talks with Captain sahab, who gave her the book; with everyone else it shows only in her counting. In chapter 4 her questions are the decisions themselves, asked plainly with no tag (rule 37), crisp and warm, never the comic one. To Nani she slows into whole, careful, polite Hindi sentences with -इए, no English and no tag. Moved, she goes very short and plain ('March. Jawaab: haan.'). Cross, she gets faster but not louder (Mausi is the one who gets louder): flat and exact, she reads out the record in two or three chained bubbles, then the book snaps shut and the ear cups go on. She talks most to you, as an equal and a rival; then to Nani, in polite Hindi.
voice.mix: Young small-town Hinglish, the way a final-year commerce student talks at home: a Hindi frame with short English clauses dropped in ('Seriously?', 'Wait, wait', 'not now', 'No way') and the everyday English verb with kar or ho ('call kiya', 'miss karungi', 'try karo', 'relax kijiye'). Her counting words are a scorer's (baar, ginti, score, total, record); the cricket words (run, over, wicket, keeper, innings) come out on cup day and with Captain sahab, never as a code for a feeling. Commerce words stay out of her speech (stock, bill, balance, hisaab, profit), so the shop family's talk does not tip into the trader idiom; 'tally' and 'total' stay because a scorer uses them. No trending slang ('literally', 'vibe', 'bestie'): her quickness is in the teasing and the counting (realism notes, section 7). The common fillers are hers as much as anyone's (arre, achha, chalo, bas, theek hai, haan), and so is everyday Hindustani (fikr, zaroor, waqt). With Nani: plain polite Hindi, आप, every word in full, no English except Nani's own nouns (doctor, BP) and the one '80, not out, Nani.' at the homecoming. With Mummy, Papa and the other elders: the same Hinglish with आप and ji, her English kept to a word or two ('Seriously, Mama ji?', 'Papa, please, not now.'); her teasing rides on counts, so it never needs a familiar 'you' to an elder. With you: तुम and 'yaar', in commands, 'who should' questions and lines where you are not the doer (rule 66). Hindi mode: natural Hindi that a reader with little English follows easily. Her English clauses turn into Hindi ('Seriously?' is 'सच में?', 'Wait, wait' is 'रुकिए, रुकिए', 'Relax' is 'आराम से'); only the loans every Hindi reader knows stay (सॉरी, थैंक यू, स्कोर, रिकॉर्ड, पार्टी, स्पीकर, and रन, विकेट on cup day), and she says तीन-ज़ीरो, not the formal तीन-शून्य (Hindi-first readers confirm). Hinglish mode: every number is a figure ('3 baar', '4 chammach'), so a number is never misread as a word. English mode: plain young Indian English, numbers as words, 'haan?' and 'yaar' kept, and 'zero' rather than the British 'nil'.
tics: The tally tease: counts someone's habit out loud, to their face, then 'haan?': 'Achha Mami, aaj ye 4 baar, haan?' | 'अच्छा मामी, आज ये चार बार, हाँ?' | 'Okay, Mami, that's four times today, haan?' Only counts, scores and totals, never an ordinal, a clock time or a price.
Ends a tease with 'haan?' | 'हाँ?', in every mode. Not on a moved line, not to Nani, and not on a chapter 4 question.
The quick English question when something happens again: 'Seriously? Phir se?' | 'सच में? फिर से?' | 'Seriously? Again?' It is how her cross run starts.
The dodge, her contradiction: asked about herself (her marks, her plans, the form), she answers with somebody else's count, a different person each time: 'Main? Papa aaj 4 baar tok chuke. Record.'
Says 'Kitaab mein.' when anyone makes a promise: it is written down now. Never after a report of harassment or a dowry demand (rule 22).
Hands a choice over with 'Faisla tumhara.' It is a test, not a shrug: she scores what you do with it.

The commentary aside, at most once a chapter: calls a small household moment live, in the present tense, like a commentator: 'Aur ye gaya!' | 'और ये गया!' | 'And there it goes!'; 'Aur Mama ji gate par! Kya entry!'
Says the feeling first, in plain words, then the joke or the fact: 'Sorry, meri galti.' before the corrected count; 'Thank you.' before the thing she is thanking you for.
When cross: faster and flatter, never louder; the record in two or three chained bubbles, then the book shut and the ear cups on.
catchphrases: 'Kitaab mein.' | 'किताब में।' | 'In the book.' (when anyone promises something; verbless, so it marks no gender)
'Seriously? Phir se?' | 'सच में? फिर से?' | 'Seriously? Again?' (new, from the readers' note; the start of her cross run, most often at Mama ji)
'Faisla tumhara.' | 'फ़ैसला तुम्हारा।' | 'Your call.' (you are not the doer; the rule 66 checker flags तुम्हारा at a sentence end and a native reader clears it, since it agrees with फ़ैसला)
voice.exclamation: 'Gazab!' | 'ग़ज़ब!' | 'Brilliant!' Kept: the readers marked it as ringing true, and it sounds like UP, which suits a junction town. Nobody else in the cast takes it as their exclamation. Bright for a good surprise (a cousin's job, a phone call, the last ball); flat and ironic for a bad one (the lights going out: 'Gazab! Batti gul, khel band.'). Typed, it stretches: 'gazabbb'. Religious meaning: none in everyday Hindi, where it means 'amazing' or 'unbelievable'. Guard: never in 'ग़ज़ब ख़ुदा का' or 'ख़ुदा का ग़ज़ब' ('God's wrath'), and never followed by any name. The English 'Brilliant!' avoids every mild word that hides a holy name (Gosh, Blimey, Crikey, Goodness). A Hindi-first and an Urdu-speaking reader confirm; fallback 'Zabardast!' | 'ज़बरदस्त!' | 'Terrific!'.
voice.sorry_thanks_love: SORRY: plain and at once, in English, then the fact put right on the spot, because she never fudges a count, her own included: 'Sorry, meri galti. 14 nahin, 15.' | 'सॉरी, मेरी ग़लती। चौदह नहीं, पंद्रह।' | 'Sorry, my mistake. Fifteen, not fourteen.' To an elder, the same words with the name ('Sorry, Papa. Meri galti.'). To Nani, in Hindi only: 'Nani, galti ho gayi. Abhi theek karti hoon.' | 'नानी, ग़लती हो गई। अभी ठीक करती हूँ।' | 'My mistake, Nani. I'll put it right now.' One sorry and no food in her hand, so it never sounds like Mausi's 'Sorry, sorry, sorry!' with a plate held out. With Captain sahab only, at most once a chapter, the scorer's sorry that is their bond: 'Mera wicket, Captain sahab.' THANKS: a plain 'Thank you', then the thing she is thanking for: to you, 'Thank you. Kal raat ki dawai tumne sambhali.' | 'थैंक यू। कल रात की दवाई तुमने सँभाली।' | 'Thanks. You handled last night's medicines.' (the ने past agrees with दवाई, so it gives you no gender). To an elder, 'Thank you, Mausa ji.' with the name. To Nani, in Hindi: 'Nani, aapne bacha liya.' | 'नानी, आपने बचा लिया।' | 'Nani, you saved me.' WHEN SHE IS THANKED: she brushes it off and puts the credit in someone else's column, which is her contradiction again: 'Arre Masterji, kuch nahin. Bas gin liya.' | 'अरे मास्टरजी, कुछ नहीं। बस गिन लिया।' | 'Oh, it's nothing, Masterji. I only counted.' With Captain sahab, in their cricket: 'Run aapka, Captain sahab. Kitaab aapne hi di thi.' LOVE: plain and short, never in a cricket code. To you at a parting: 'Jaldi aana, yaar. Main din ginungi.' | 'जल्दी आना, यार। मैं दिन गिनूँगी।' | 'Come back soon, yaar. I'll be counting the days.' (a real idiom in both languages, her counting turned tender). After a hard week: 'Baitho, yaar. Tumne bahut kiya.' The one love line in cricket is the birthday saying everyone in India knows, once a year, when Nani comes home: '80, not out, Nani.' | 'अस्सी, नॉट आउट, नानी।' | 'Eighty, not out, Nani.'

Short English clauses: 'Seriously?', 'Wait, wait', 'not now', 'No way', 'Okay'
An English verb with kar or ho: 'call kiya', 'miss karungi', 'try karo', 'relax kijiye'
Counting words: baar, ginti, ginna, score, total, tally, record | बार, गिनती, गिनना, स्कोर, रिकॉर्ड
Count shapes: '4 baar', 'ye 4', '3 mein 0', 'aapke 42, mere 42', and '[total], not out' (Nani's homecoming only)
Cricket words on cup day and with Captain sahab: run, over, wicket, keeper, fielder, ball | रन, ओवर, विकेट, कीपर, फ़ील्डर, गेंद
the book, meaning her scorebook: 'kitaab' | 'किताब'; 'Kitaab mein.'
'Faisla tumhara.'; with Captain sahab only, 'Mera wicket.' and 'Run aapka.'
'Gazab!' (her exclamation), 'haan?' (her tease tag), 'yaar' (to you), 'oye' (to you, rarely, mostly typed)
'Ji nahin' for a polite no to an elder
The everyday fillers, like everyone in the house: arre, achha, chalo, bas, theek hai, haan; and everyday Hindustani such as fikr and zaroor
Real everyday idioms, never proverbs (those are Nani's): 'batti gul', 'din ginna'
never: bhai, bro, didi, bhaiya, beta or any word that gives you a gender (rule 8)
तू to anyone, or a तू command such as 'bata' or 'sun'; she says बताओ and सुनो
a Hindi line to you that the rule 66 checker cannot clear: no -ोगे/-ोगी, no थके/थकी, no कौन जाएगा?, no खाते/खाती रहो
'yaar' or 'oye' to an elder
clock times, durations or prices, in speech or typing (Papa owns minutes; prices leave everyone's speech); her numbers are counts, scores and totals only
ordinals: teesri baar, chauthi baar, pehli baar, 3rd (matrix 2.15); she says '3 baar'
commerce words as her idiom: stock, bill, balance, hisaab, profit, udhaar

cricket as a code for a feeling with anyone but Captain sahab: no 'Run tumhara', 'Innings abhi baaki', 'Kya debut!', 'Extras', 'Over poora' or 'Match tie'. 'Mera wicket' and 'Run aapka' go to Captain sahab only, each at most once a chapter

the bare call 'Not out.', 'Next ball', 'Well played', 'Well fielded', 'Front foot', 'Straight bat', the toss call or any umpire's verdict (all Captain sahab's); 'not out' only after a total, and only for Nani

other people's set phrases, tags and exclamations (the common fillers are everyone's and are not on this list): Mausi's 'Suno, suno, suno!', 'Sorry, sorry, sorry!', 'hai na?' and 'Haaye'; Captain sahab's 'Arre waah.'; Nani's 'Bas.' as a closing word and 'Baap re'; Mausa ji's one-word 'Theek.'; Mama ji's 'Pakka?' at the end of a worry and 'Oho'; Mami's 'Correct?' or 'Sahi?' tag and 'Ish'; Mummy's 'Had hai'; Papa's 'Reached?'; your 'Pehle ___', 'Badhiya.' and 'Sab set.'
'Badhai ho' (Mummy's, if the owner allows it) and 'Mubarak ho' (left unused, so the congratulation leans to no community); her congratulation is 'Gazab! Party kab hai?'
any religious word or exclamation (rule 3; the list in matrix 2.13), any caste word, any brand
slang or English to Nani, apart from Nani's own nouns and the one '80, not out'
trending slang such as 'literally', 'vibe', 'delulu' or 'bestie'; her quickness is in the teasing and the counting (realism notes, section 7)
'the youngest' about herself, except to refuse it
'captain' as a job word on a chapter 4 card or question (rule 36: in Hindi the word is Captain sahab's title)
'sharp', already worn out by three askers
'too emotional', 'drama', 'bossy', 'argues', or any note word read as sexist on sight; nothing about women or men in general (rule 22)
the name, or a note word, of anyone on a decision's cards before or during that decision (rule 36)

any doubt of a report of harassment or a dowry demand, the word 'misunderstanding', or any ask for proof ('saboot', 'proof', 'likhit mein', 'in writing') near a report beat (rule 22); she writes it down exactly as it was said, and she believes it
'well done', 'oops', 'sorry' or 'please' in a chapter outcome line (rule 64)
a year on screen (rule 2)
a spoken bubble over 10 words (rule 62); a long run becomes more bubbles
address: Nani: 'Nani' | 'नानी', आप, polite Hindi only, -इए forms. Nani calls her 'Tinku', and 'scorer' | 'स्कोरर' only when the scorebook proves her right (Nani's note).

Mummy: 'Mummy' | 'मम्मी', आप, the same as to Papa, so respect is equal between the parents (realism notes 1.1, source [6]). When Mummy is cross she calls her 'Tinku ji', with आप, and Tinku knows at once that she is in trouble.
Mama ji: 'Mama ji' | 'मामा जी', आप. Mami: 'Mami' | 'मामी', आप.
Mausi: 'Mausi' | 'मौसी', आप. Mausa ji: 'Mausa ji' | 'मौसा जी', आप.
Masterji: 'Masterji' | 'मास्टरजी', आप. Captain sahab: 'Captain sahab' | 'कप्तान साहब', आप.

You (the player): mostly no address word. When she wants one, 'yaar' | 'यार', the everyday word that young women and men all over north India use to a sibling or a friend, which marks no gender (the owner and the readers clear it under rules 8 and 66). 'oye' | 'ओए' only now and then, mostly typed, never to an elder. तुम, because 'elder' in her file means a generation up (Hindi-first readers settle it). Her Hindi to you is only commands (उठो, चुनो, बैठो, आना), 'who should' questions (कौन देखे?) and lines where you are not the doer (फ़ैसला तुम्हारा, दवाई तुमने सँभाली). Never बेटा, भैया or दीदी. You call her 'scorer'.
People on the cards: first names only, and only in rule 38's fixed line after a pick, never before or during a decision.
While rulebook Q7 is open, nobody calls Tinku 'beta' either, so you are not the only one without a pet name.
samples: Announcing (the opening, the kitchen, January; kept): English 'August 15. Lane cup. I'm scoring.' | Hinglish '15 August. Gali ka cup. Score mera.' | Hindi '15 अगस्त। गली का कप। स्कोर मेरा।' (a date, not a clock: the cup is the year's deadline)
Waking you (chapter 4, 4.02): English 'Up, yaar! Come on, it's cup day.' | Hinglish 'Utho, yaar! Chalo, cup ka din.' | Hindi 'उठो, यार! चलो, कप का दिन।' (a command, rule 66 clear; no figure)

Asking (chapter 4, decision 2, to you; plain, no tag, rule 37): English 'Three fielders, one a keeper. Pick fast.' | Hinglish '3 fielder, 1 keeper. Jaldi chuno.' | Hindi 'तीन फ़ील्डर, एक कीपर। जल्दी चुनो।' (the continuity read's wording; the toss stays Captain sahab's)
Handing over (chapter 4, 4.04, kept): English 'Two targets. Today, your call.' | Hinglish '2 target. Aaj faisla tumhara.' | Hindi 'दो टारगेट। आज फ़ैसला तुम्हारा।'

Everyone aboard (chapter 1, the coach, to Papa, who has just counted; replaces 'Over poora'): English 'Everyone's in, Papa. I counted too.' | Hinglish 'Sab andar, Papa. Maine bhi gine.' | Hindi 'सब अंदर, पापा। मैंने भी गिने।' (no figure; their nod across the coach is the rest of it)

Teasing Papa (chapter 1's platform, kept): English 'Papa, the train's on time. Shall I write that down?' | Hinglish 'Papa, gaadi time pe hai. Kitaab mein likhoon?' | Hindi 'पापा, गाड़ी टाइम पर है। किताब में लिखूँ?'

A tally tease (a family function, to Mami, who has raised the accounts course again): English 'Okay, Mami, that's four times today, haan?' | Hinglish 'Achha Mami, aaj ye 4 baar, haan?' | Hindi 'अच्छा मामी, आज ये चार बार, हाँ?'

Teasing Captain sahab (chapter 4, kept): English 'Your one trial again, Captain sahab? Eleven times this season.' | Hinglish 'Phir wahi trial, Captain sahab? Is season 11 baar.' | Hindi 'फिर वही ट्रायल, कप्तान साहब? इस सीज़न ग्यारह बार।' (no year on screen, rule 2)

Taking a promise (chapter 5, Mama ji says he will come again in March): English 'March, Mama ji? Fine. It's in the book.' | Hinglish 'Mama ji, aapne March bola? Theek hai. Kitaab mein.' | Hindi 'मामा जी, आपने मार्च बोला? ठीक है। किताब में।'

A commentary aside, her joke, the chapter's one (chapter 5, Mama ji's car at Nani's gate): English 'And here's Mama ji at the gate! What an entry!' | Hinglish 'Aur Mama ji gate par! Kya entry!' | Hindi 'और मामा जी गेट पर! क्या एंट्री!' (no figure)

Worrying (chapter 2's night, to you): English 'Yaar, Nani's medicines, three a day. Who's checking tonight?' | Hinglish 'Yaar, Nani ki dawai din mein 3. Aaj raat kaun dekhe?' | Hindi 'यार, नानी की दवाई दिन में तीन। आज रात कौन देखे?' (a 'who should' question, rule 66)

Comforting you (the end of the flood week): English 'Sit, yaar. You've done enough.' / 'I'll do tonight's count.' | Hinglish 'Baitho, yaar. Tumne bahut kiya.' / 'Aaj raat ginti meri.' | Hindi 'बैठो, यार। तुमने बहुत किया।' / 'आज रात गिनती मेरी।' (किया agrees with बहुत and मेरी with गिनती; both flagged, both cleared)

Comforting Nani (after the fall; Hindi words even in Hinglish mode): English 'Nani, you sit. Don't worry, I've got your medicines.' | Hinglish 'Nani, aap baithiye. Fikr mat kijiye, dawai main doongi.' | Hindi 'नानी, आप बैठिए। फ़िक्र मत कीजिए, दवाई मैं दूँगी।'

Carrom with Nani (Nani cheats, and Tinku sees): English 'Nani, you nudged that coin with your finger. I saw.' | Hinglish 'Nani, ye goti aapne ungli se khiskayi. Maine dekha.' | Hindi 'नानी, ये गोटी आपने उँगली से खिसकाई। मैंने देखा।' (polite आपने, no tag, the tease in her eyes)

Settling the flood argument (chapter 3, to Mummy as the shutter goes up; replaces 'Match tie'): English 'Mummy, your forty-two, my forty-two. We're both right, haan?' | Hinglish 'Mummy, aapke 42, mere 42. Dono sahi, haan?' | Hindi 'मम्मी, आपके बयालीस, मेरे बयालीस। दोनों सही, हाँ?' (both counts were right)

Calming Mausi (the wedding week, Mausi asking about the sweets three questions at a time): English 'Relax, Mausi. I've got it.' | Hinglish 'Mausi, relax kijiye. Main dekh leti hoon.' | Hindi 'मौसी, आराम से। मैं देख लेती हूँ।' (an English verb with kar, in the polite form)

Holding out the phone (any evening, to you): English 'Yaar, Mama ji called again.' / 'Asking for you, as usual.' | Hinglish 'Yaar, Mama ji ne phir call kiya.' / 'Tumhe hi pooch rahe the.' | Hindi 'यार, मामा जी ने फिर फ़ोन किया।' / 'तुम्हें ही पूछ रहे थे।' (Mama ji is the doer of both verbs; flagged, cleared)

Sorry (cup morning, to Captain sahab, the water bottles left at home; their cricket, once this chapter): English 'My wicket, Captain sahab. I'll fetch the bottles now.' | Hinglish 'Mera wicket, Captain sahab. Bottlein abhi laati hoon.' | Hindi 'मेरा विकेट, कप्तान साहब। बोतलें अभी लाती हूँ।'

Thanks (to you, the morning after you sat up with Nani's medicines; the readers' line): English 'Thanks. You handled last night's medicines.' | Hinglish 'Thank you. Kal raat ki dawai tumne sambhali.' | Hindi 'थैंक यू। कल रात की दवाई तुमने सँभाली।' (the ने past agrees with दवाई; flagged, cleared)

Being thanked (the flood week, to Masterji, after she counted his wet cloth): English 'Oh, it's nothing, Masterji. I only counted.' | Hinglish 'Arre Masterji, kuch nahin. Bas gin liya.' | Hindi 'अरे मास्टरजी, कुछ नहीं। बस गिन लिया।'

Love (chapter 2's end, Nani home from the ward; kept; waits on rulebook Q5 and Q11): English 'Eighty, not out, Nani.' | Hinglish '80, not out, Nani.' | Hindi 'अस्सी, नॉट आउट, नानी।' (the one 'not out' she says, after a total)

Saying no (chapter 5, to Mami, about the accounts course; kept): English 'No, Mami. I already keep score. Ten seasons now.' | Hinglish 'Ji nahin, Mami. Score toh rakhti hoon. 10 season se.' | Hindi 'जी नहीं, मामी। स्कोर तो रखती हूँ। दस सीज़न से।'

Dodging Papa (dinner, when he brings up the railway exam): English 'Papa, please, not now. We'll talk about the exam later.' | Hinglish 'Papa, please, not now. Exam ki baat baad mein.' | Hindi 'पापा, प्लीज़, अभी नहीं। परीक्षा की बात बाद में।'

Her contradiction (Mausi asks about her marks): English 'My marks, Mausi? Mausa ji's said "Hmm" nine times today.' | Hinglish 'Mere marks, Mausi? Mausa ji ne aaj 9 baar "Hmm" kaha.' | Hindi 'मेरे नंबर, मौसी? मौसा जी ने आज नौ बार "हम्म" कहा।'

Losing her temper (to Mama ji, when he calls her 'the youngest' once too often; three chained bubbles, fast and flat, then the book shut and the ear cups on): English 'Mama ji, seriously? "The youngest" again?' / 'Twelve times this year. Your promises? Zero out of three.' / 'I'm the scorer, Mama ji. The scorer.' | Hinglish 'Mama ji, seriously? Phir se "sabse chhoti"?' / 'Is saal 12 baar. Aapke vaade? 3 mein 0.' / 'Scorer hoon main, Mama ji. Scorer.' | Hindi 'मामा जी, सच में? फिर से "सबसे छोटी"?' / 'इस साल बारह बार। आपके वादे? तीन में ज़ीरो।' / 'स्कोरर हूँ मैं, मामा जी। स्कोरर।'
